extracted.intended_audience: general readers of moral and literary essays; aspiring actors, playwrights, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for theatrical performance and dramatic writing embedded in moral essays; also broader counsel on friendship, thought, and habit that informs character and conduct in writing. Useful for critics, dramatists, and creative writers learning craft and critical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining friendship: similarity and intercourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship depends on a 'similitude of manners and sentiment' and regular intercourse; meeting after long separation often disappoints because 'different scenes have made different impressions' and likeness that once confirmed mutual approbation is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectations of revived attraction on reunion are frequently disappointed; maintain regular contact and similarity of manners to sustain friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition of interest undermines friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Friendship is often destroyed by opposition of interest, not only by the ponderous and visible interest which the desire of wealth and greatness forms and maintains, but by a thousand secret and slight competitions...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to small, private ambitions or petty prizes that create rivalry; once a vulnerable point is found it will be feared and resentment will smoulder—so avoid actions that expose or exploit such vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarrels begun in jest may escalate irreparably
rubrics_metrics.description: A dispute begun in jest can be 'continued by the desire of conquest, till vanity kindles into rage, and opposition rankles into enmity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and participants should be aware that petty antagonism can grow into lasting enmity; immediate tempering and willingness to reconcile after a tumult are necessary but often insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual decay is the deadliest threat to friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The most fatal disease of friendship is gradual decay, or dislike hourly increased by causes too slender for complaint, and too numerous for removal.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger or injury can be remedied; but the silent diminution of mutual desire to please is usually hopeless—cultivate attentiveness and mutual pleasure to prevent slow estrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought requires subjects/materials to arise
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘To every act a subject is required. He that thinks must think upon something.’ Thought is not an automatic constant; minds without impressions, experience, or design may lack thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide experiences, reading, and engagements as 'materials' for reflection; encourage varied ideas and stimuli to sustain contemplative life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid torpid insensibility; value diversified ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A life without varied ideas is compared to a carcass: 'He that lives in torpid insensibility, wants nothing of a carcass but putrefaction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative writers should seek diversified impressions and interests to avoid dullness of mind and to provide fodder for reflection and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's duty: distinguish error from inability
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The care of the critick should be to distinguish errour from inability, faults of inexperience from defects of nature.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should be charitable where faults are due to inexperience and surgical where defects are innate; aim to instruct and correct rather than to humiliate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible faults in young actors (tolerable, correctable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faults such as 'variation of gesture, and flexion of voice', 'action irregular and turbulent', 'vociferation vehement and confused' are often remedies of inexperience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These defects should be initially pardoned and later censured with gentleness and candour; practical stage experience will generally correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intolerable actor defects (grounds for dismissal)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If in an actor there appears an utter vacancy of meaning, a frigid equality, a stupid languor, a torpid apathy, the greatest kindness that can be shown him is a speedy sentence of expulsion.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between correctable inexperience and incurable absence of expressive capacity; the latter warrants removal for the good of the play and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic craft vs natural gift
rubrics_metrics.description: While 'the power of distinguishing and discriminating comick characters, or of filling tragedy with poetical images, must be the gift of nature', 'the art of dramatick disposition, the contexture of the scenes, the opposition of characters, the involution of the plot, the expedients of suspension, and the stratagems of surprise, are to be learned by practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspiring dramatists should be encouraged: innate genius helps, but the structural and technical skills of drama are learnable through practice and study—do not discourage novices for lacking natural genius alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproof should target vice, not petty failings
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Reproof should not exhaust its power upon petty failings; let it watch diligently against the incursion of vice, and leave foppery and futility to die of themselves.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving feedback or editing, prioritize curbing morally harmful habits and serious faults; allow minor vanities and silliness to fade rather than burning energy on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical method for changing habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Bacon: 'He that endeavours to free himself from an ill habit, must not change too much at a time, lest he should be discouraged by difficulty; nor too little, for then he will make but slow advances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend gradual but significant reform—neither overwhelming nor trivial steps—to effectively change character or practice; early caution preserves freedom from bad habits.
